newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Weak Thai U.S. dlr debt market worsened by Moody's.
newsitem.headline: Weak Thai U.S. dlr debt market worsened by Moody's.

text.p: Thai debt paper weakened modestly in an already depressed market after Moody's Investors Service said it may cut the kingdom's sovereign ratings, traders in Hong Kong said on Friday.
"A couple of days ago, prices were marked down, but today we are seeing some of those prices actually being hit," said a trader at a U.S. bank.
Moody's said it might cut Thailand's A2 long-term foreign currency debt and deposit ratings.
The review was prompted by concerns regarding the soundness of Thailand's financial sector as well as by constraints on macroeconomic policy-making, Moody's said.

The rating agency also put on review for possible downgrade the A2 long-term foreign currency ratings of Bangkok Bank, Export-Import Bank of Thailand, Industrial Finance Corp of Thailand, Siam Commercial Bank and Thai Farmers Bank.
Traders said that while prices were quoted and some offers were taken, most players still remained sidelined.
"For the foreign currency debt, there hasn't been much selling at all," said a trader at a European bank.
"Thailand's problems already have been discounted in that market and for certain names there has been widening pressure for quite a while now," he said.

Standard and Poor's Corp told Reuters it had no plans to downgrade Thailand, reiterating its view that the sovereign was strong enough to weather problems in the banking sector. Traders said some of the A2 rated floating rate issues of Thai banks with tenors of three to five years were indicated at about five basis points wider than on Thursday.

Traders said the recent floating rate certificate of deposit issue of Thai Farmers Bank was indicated in the mid-30s over the London Interbank Offered Rate, a few basis points wider than on Thursday and several wider than the 27 basis points all-in it offered at launch in January.
Many bankers said Thai paper had been priced too tightly and that the recent weakening in prices was a better reflection of market sentiment.
The outstanding debt issues of Thailand's lower-rated borrowers have been harder hit by the country's economic troubles and weak banking sector.

For example, Baa2-rated Siam City Bank, which was not put on watch, has a floating rate note issue due 2001 and puttable in 1999 that was trading around 80 basis points over LIBOR on Thursday but has widened out to 90-100 basis points.
Those notes offered a 53.3 basis points all-in return when they were launched in January 1996.

In contrast, traders said IFCT's latest bond, a Euro 144a bond due in 2007, was trading at 85 basis points over comparable U.S. Treasuries, wider than the 80 basis points it touched at its height but tighter than the 90 basis points it yielded at launch in early January 1997.
"In the Eurobonds, we're not seeing any dramatic movements, but the phone isn't really running off the hook with people trying to bid the paper," said a U.S. bank trader.
But some Eurobonds have shown significant volatility.
